title: Science and faith
hook: Muslims who see the study of nature as reading Allah's signs

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslims as minorities, and your line: faith as a minority. Abyssinia, the best of neighbors. Were you someone's good neighbor yesterday? Today a new stretch begins: questions of today. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

"Will they not regard the camels, how they are created?" That's a line of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, from surah al-Ghashiyah. It doesn't argue. It points. And then it keeps pointing: at the sky, how it is raised; at the mountains, how they are set; at the earth, how it is spread out. A scripture that stops in the middle of its message to say: look at the animal in front of you, and ask how it was made. Today opens a new part of the path, questions of today, with a question people of faith keep asking. What happens when a person of faith picks up a microscope?
screen: `REGARD THE CAMELS.` → `THE SKY, THE MOUNTAINS, THE EARTH.` → `FAITH PICKS UP A MICROSCOPE.`

segments.voice: First, a word that does double duty. In the Qur'an, ayah, plural ayat, is used for the verses of the scripture, and it is also used for signs in the world. In surah Al 'Imran, in paraphrase, the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for people of understanding. Some Muslim writers put it simply: there are two books, the book revealed and the book of creation, and both are read for signs. Second, an invitation to look. Surah al-Ghashiyah points at camels, sky, mountains, earth. Other verses point at rain, at bees, at the stages of a child in the womb, at the variety of languages and colors. In Ibn Majah, in paraphrase, the Prophet, peace be upon him, calls seeking knowledge a duty on every Muslim. Third, a history with practical roots. Finding the direction of prayer, the qibla, and the times of the prayers took careful work with the sky. Tradition remembers scholars like Ibn al-Haytham, who studied how light and sight work, and Ibn Sina, who wrote on medicine. Fourth, the questions that are still open. Muslims today work across the sciences, and they discuss how faith and findings fit together. Some writers look for scientific wonders foretold in the Qur'an. Other scholars caution against this, because science revises itself, and they would rather not tie a verse to a theory that may change. Some see no conflict to resolve at all: for them, studying a cell or a star is reading signs, and the reading itself is worship.
screen: `AYAH: A VERSE, AND A SIGN.` · `REGARD: CAMELS, RAIN, BEES, STARS.` · `THE QIBLA AND THE SKY.` · `OPEN QUESTIONS, HONESTLY KEPT.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one scientific wonder. Begin with the one closest to you. Settle, and breathe. Notice the breath itself: air moving in, the chest rising, something in you taking what it needs from the air without being asked. Stay with that for a few breaths, curious rather than busy. Then look at your own hand for a moment, the creases, the joints, the way it closes. If you pray, you can look at your hand the way the verse looks at the camel, and ask how it was made. Afterward, read about one thing in nature you've never understood, and learn how it works. The bell holds the time.
Science and faith. For Muslims who read the world as ayat, signs, studying nature is a way of reading the book of creation alongside the book revealed. Today's word.

Your line: science reads signs. Today, find one small natural thing, a leaf, a bird, a cloud, and ask how it was made, then go and find out. Tomorrow, medicine and fasting. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.
